It also provides a siting rubric that can allow multiple stakeholder participation and publicly defensible guidelines for when projects are selected, deemphasized, or eliminated. 21 F3 provides direct public benefit by centering its solution sets on vulnerable populations, offering access to clean energy and community benefits. The community-based research detailed methodologies that can be applied by governmental and organizational staff to deepen community engagement. From its onset, F3 recognized financial limitations that would prevent a municipality from creating broad solar and storage solutions to meet the resilient power needs of an entire community. This was found to especially be the case when grid outages and major natural disasters are more limited in the Midwest compared to large ongoing wildfire and hurricane risks experienced elsewhere in the country, thus limiting return on investment or upfront willingness to pay for resilience premiums. Determining the most vulnerable populations, weather event contexts, and negative impacts related to grid outages through community-based participatory research, and then working with community members and stakeholders to identify and implement individual and community-based approaches provides forward progress while more costly renewable projects are contemplated, designed, and implemented. Ultimately, Duluth will be a more resilient community during grid disruptions as community identified support systems, such as resilience and preparedness classes, individual emergency power plans, and expanding uptake of renter’s insurance to bridge recovery gaps. This provides an option to build resilience even if renewable projects are never built. During the performance period of this grant, two significant changes occurred. The first was staffing changes at the City of Duluth that increases capacity limitations for project implementation. The second major change was the federal shift away from solar development as preferred energy policy and modifications to anticipated federal roles in disaster response. Both of these changes underscore the importance of the F3 approach that deeply engaged community stakeholders and delivered solutions sets that were not dependent solely on renewable incentives or development. By expanding those potentially involved in delivering resilience solutions, greater overall community capacity can be built. In many ways, F3 provided a community-derived answer to the question, “With limited resources, what are the most important resilience actions to implement.” The answer resulted in greater interest in community knowledge exchange and very targeted individual action than larger, more expensive renewable projects. Despite these challenges and conclusions, F3 accomplished a replicable, open-source toolkit that can be adopted by smaller municipalities across cold-climate regions, an expansion of energy resilience planning and preparation of communities for extreme weather events and grid disruptions, a methodology for creating community-based minimum resilience standards to protect a community’s most vulnerable residents, and renewable siting and evaluation tools to lessen the burden on capacity-limited communities. 22 Path Forward The City of Duluth’s initial interest in the RACER grant was to vet and prioritize projects for implementation, as resilience is advanced through actual projects, not just project plans.
